items.title: 2.7.2 Distribution of electrons in subshells and orbitals: the Aufbau principle

source_refs.note: Topic 2.7.2, printed pages 34-36: the Aufbau principle, Table 2.6 and the energy order (Figure 2.12).

blocks.text: Following rules are applied to fill the orbitals of multi-electron atoms.
Aufbau principle is also known as the building up principle.

blocks.title: Aufbau principle
blocks.text: This principle says that the subshells in an atom are filled with electrons in an increasing order of their energy values.
Now, question arises that how to arrange the subshells energy wise.

Since, the energy of a subshell in the absence of any magnetic field, depends upon the principal quantum number (n) and the azimuthal quantum number (ℓ), hence the order of filling subshells with electrons may be obtained from the summation (n + ℓ). (n + ℓ) values are given in Table 2.6.

blocks.caption: Table 2.6 (n + ℓ) values of various sub-shells.

items: The subshell having lower (n + ℓ) value has lower energy and is filled first. For example, 4s orbital has (n + ℓ) = 4 + 0 = 4 and 3d orbital has (n + ℓ) = 3+2 = 5. Since (n + ℓ) value of 4s orbital is lower than that of 3d, hence 4s subshell has lower energy than 3d and 4s will be filled first.

In case there are two subshells are having equal (n + ℓ) values, then the subshell with lower ‘n’ value will be filled first. For example, both 4p and 3d subshells have n+l value equal to 5 (4p=4+1=5) and (3d = 3+2=5); 3d subshell will be preferred to be filled because of its low n value.

blocks.text: According to this rule the energy wise arrangement of orbitals should be.

blocks.alt: Subshells drawn as rows of boxes, one box per orbital, placed higher for higher energy: 1s, 2s, 2p, 3s, 3p, 4s, 3d, 4p, 5s, 4d, 5p, 6s, 4f, 5d, 6p, 7s, 5f, 6d, 7p from bottom to top. An arrow on the left marks the orbital filling sequence and a coloured arrow beside it marks increasing energy.
blocks.caption: Fig 2.12: The diagram shows the energy of each subshell. Each box on the diagram represents an atomic orbital (original drawing after the textbook's Fig 2.12).
